assessmentSettings.questionNumberingInstructions: Use each question's explicit feedbackLabel and questionNumber for student-facing feedback. These are one-based numbers in the full assessment. Internal answer identifiers such as A4 are not question numbers. Do not infer a number from an internal identifier or renumber a subset of questions. Match the response to questionId and its prompt; if they conflict, flag the mismatch rather than guess.

feedbackPolicy.instructions: Begin the overall comment with varied, brief encouragement naming only skills demonstrated in this submission. Then address only missed items, using the actual Question N label and one short correction per item, at most 25 words excluding the label. End with a freshly written positive sentence specific to this student's work; do not recycle a standard closing or use "Keep up the effort." Do not include scores, percentages, points earned or deducted, internal IDs, or em dashes. Question numbers and physics values are allowed. Never invent evidence, a mistake, or mastery. If every answer is correct, give only the evidence-based opening and specific closing. Per-question fields contain only the relevant correction; do not repeat the opening and closing in each field.

assessmentSettings.gradingCalibration: Grade the understanding shown. Accept equivalent wording, reasonable rounding and simulation precision; do not demand repeated units already supplied by a blank or an explanation that the blank did not request. For written responses, credit correct concepts, methods and consistent follow-through. Deduct for the original error without repeatedly penalizing its correctly carried-forward consequences. A minor omission is not a wholly incorrect answer. Judge only requested evidence; a clear qualitative graph change is valid when the prompt allows it. Preserve deductions for materially wrong values, misconceptions and missing required work. Binary completion items remain binary. Check the published assignment version and its actual question numbers before grading.

questions.answerReference:

b. Total distance stays the same as time increases.
*c. Total distance is proportional to time squared, so doubling the time quadruples the distance.
d. Total distance is proportional to the square root of time, so quadrupling the time doubles the distance.

questions.prompt: Galileo studied acceleration by rolling balls down a gentle slope. Why was this easier than measuring a ball dropped straight down?

feedback.whenCorrect: Good work! You demonstrated a solid grasp of Galileo's timing method.
feedback.whenIncorrect: Think about the difficulty of timing a very fast fall with the instruments available to Galileo.
feedback.usage: Use only when points were lost; adapt to the actual error and keep the response within the feedback policy.

questions.answerReference:
*a. The slower motion gave him more time to measure how the ball's speed changed.
b. The slope made the ball move at constant speed, so no timing was needed.
c. Gravity stopped acting on the ball while it was on the slope.
d. The distance alone told him the acceleration, so he did not need to measure time.

questions.prompt: Part 3 of 3 - Average acceleration. Use the speeds you calculated in Parts 1 and 2. Here is the motion equation: v_last = v_first + a * delta_t. Rearranged: a = (v_last - v_first) / delta_t, where a is acceleration and delta_t is the time between the speeds. For constant acceleration, an interval's average speed equals its speed at the midpoint. Our midpoint times are 0.05 s and 0.65 s, so delta_t = 0.60 s. Subtract the first speed from the last, then divide by 0.60 s. Enter the acceleration in m/s^2, taking downward as positive.

feedback.whenCorrect: Well done! Your answers show a clear understanding of acceleration from average interval speeds.
feedback.whenIncorrect: Subtract 0.49 m/s from 6.37 m/s, then divide by 0.60 s between the midpoint times. Do not divide by 0.1 s or 0.7 s.
feedback.usage: Use only when points were lost; adapt to the actual error and keep the response within the feedback policy.
